reading.title: The Five Senses 1: a sensory exhibit
reading.text: At an adult science exhibit, a tutor uses eye and ear models. The eye supports vision. Its pupil admits light, its lens focuses light, and its retina detects it. The cornea forms the clear front surface, while the optic nerve carries visual information to the brain. Color vision distinguishes colors, depth perception helps judge distance, and peripheral vision notices objects beside the direction of gaze. In the ear, an eardrum vibrates and a cochlea helps turn sound into nerve signals. Pitch describes how high or low a sound is.

reading.title: The Five Senses 2: a sensory exhibit
reading.text: The sound demonstration stays at a comfortable volume. The tutor explains frequency as the number of repeating vibrations each second, and shows how a vibration can produce sound. An echo is heard after sound reflects from a surface. The auditory nerve carries hearing information. At another table, a nose model shows a nostril and the nasal cavity. Olfactory means related to smell. Visitors discuss a coffee aroma, a flower fragrance, and an animal’s scent. Odor is a general word; stench is unpleasant, and pungent describes a sharp strong smell or taste.

reading.title: The Five Senses 4: a sensory exhibit
reading.text: Visitors describe a smooth stone and a rough wood sample. A soft cushion differs from a hard wooden chair. They use bright and dark for light levels, and loud and quiet for sound levels. Fragrant describes a pleasant smell, while stinky describes an unpleasant one. Delicious expresses a positive personal judgment about food; bland means it has little flavor. Pain, tickle, and itch name different sensations. The exhibit’s photographs support objects and settings, but the written examples establish sensations, smells, tastes, and personal opinions.
